desc:
In one operation you pick an element of nums and replace it, in the same position, by two positive integers whose sum is that element. For example [3, 9, 3] may become [3, 3, 6, 3] by splitting 9 into 3 and 6 (you choose the order of the two new elements). New elements can be split again.

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make nums non-decreasing (nums[i] ≤ nums[i+1] for all i).

[3, 9, 3] -> 2   ([3, 3, 3, 3, 3])
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] -> 0
[5, 4] -> 1   ([2, 3, 4])

In the last example, 5 is split into 2 and 3 (one operation), giving [2, 3, 4].
hints: The last element never needs to change, since there is nothing to its right. Work backwards: what does each element have to be compared to?

Every element must be broken into parts that are all at most the smallest part of the element to its right. You want as few parts as possible, and among those the smallest part as large as possible, since it becomes the limit for the element on the left.

With last the minimum of the right neighbour after its splitting and value x: if x ≤ last nothing to do (last = x). Otherwise use k = ceil(x / last) parts (cost k - 1) and split them as evenly as possible; the smallest part is x // k, which becomes the new last.
editorial: Process the array from right to left and maintain last, the smallest value among the pieces of the element to the right (after splitting it). For the current value x: if x ≤ last it is already fine, and last becomes x.

Otherwise every piece of x must be at most last, so at least k = ceil(x / last) pieces are needed, costing k - 1 operations. Using exactly k pieces, make them as equal as possible: the smallest piece is then x // k, the largest possible minimum for k pieces. Update last = x // k. (All pieces are at most ceil(x / k) ≤ last.)

The two greedy choices are justified together: fewer pieces never hurt later steps because a larger minimum gives the left neighbour more room, and splitting into more than k pieces only adds cost and lowers the minimum. Total work O(n) with O(1) extra memory. The answer is at most about 10<sup>9</sup>, so it fits in 32 bits.
